# 4thandgoal

This repo holds three apps. The site and the pipeline each have a CLAUDE.md with its own commands and rules. Read the one for the app you change.

- [Site](apps/site/README.md) in `apps/site/` is the Next.js site. Its build copies `clients/<slug>/published/` of one client into `public/` and renders each `page.json` and its images.
- [Pipeline](apps/pipeline/README.md) in `apps/pipeline/` is the Python pipeline. It builds each week and publishes it into `clients/<slug>/published/`.
- [API](apps/api/README.md) in `apps/api/` serves the trade analyzer and deploys to Fly. Its product code imports no pipeline code. Run `make help` in it.

For module ownership, follow root instructions → app README → owner README → module and test.
Choose the responsibility in the app map, then follow its owner links.

The root holds one uv workspace and one pnpm workspace, each with one lock file: `uv.lock` and `pnpm-lock.yaml`.
Run `uv sync --all-packages` and `pnpm install` at the root. A member runs with `uv run --exact --package <name>`.

## Style

Write all output in Simplified Technical English. Rules: `~/.claude/rules/communication/simplified-technical-english.md`. Active voice, present tense, one instruction per sentence, 20 words or fewer, no `-ing` as a verb, plain words. Code, technical names, and quoted output are exempt.

## Records

- `GLOSSARY.md` holds the terms of both apps, one section per app, and the workflow terms. Each term has one meaning.
- `docs/adr/` holds one ADR series for both apps. `docs/adr/README.md` maps each old app number to its new number.

## The flow

ADRs 0018 to 0021 and ADR 0026 set the flow. ADR 0026 supersedes ADR 0020. The spec `.scratch/one/` builds it, so its own tickets still merge to `main` as before.

1. `main` is the record branch. No agent commits on `main` or pushes to `main` (ADR 0019).
2. A spec branch is named `<slug>` and starts from `main`.
3. A ticket branch is named `<slug>-<NN>`. It is local, starts from the spec branch, and has its own worktree.
4. A ticket merges into its spec branch with `git merge --no-edit`, after the check passes.
5. One pull request goes from the spec branch to `main`, as a squash merge.
6. An agent records the evidence of each acceptance test `AT-<n>`. The agent gives no test verdict.
7. A fresh subagent, the Judge, gives PASS, FAIL, or BLOCKED for each test in `VERDICTS.md`. A check blocks the merge until each test has PASS. A FAIL from Brian in a PR comment overrides the Judge (ADR 0026).

The weekly `publish` is the one exception. It may push to `main`, and it may stage only `clients/<slug>/published/<season>/`, `clients/<slug>/data/<season>/`, and `clients/<slug>/build/<season>/`.

The repo plugin `4ag` takes an idea to a merged spec. Run its skills in this order. Brian approves the output of each of steps 2 to 4.

1. `4ag:plan <outcome statement>` writes the map and the decision tickets. `4ag:plan <feature>` clears one decision ticket per session.
2. `4ag:to-spec <feature>` writes `PRD.md`.
3. `4ag:to-acceptance <feature>` writes `ACCEPTANCE.md`.
4. `4ag:to-tickets <feature>` writes the tickets and the `state.md` row.
5. `4ag:implement <feature>` builds each ticket on its ticket branch, merges it into the spec branch, records the evidence in `EVIDENCE.md`, has the Judge write `VERDICTS.md`, and opens one PR to `main`.
6. Brian posts no comment unless he gives a FAIL. `4ag:review <PR number>` does one round of feedback per run. The check `verdict` passes when each test has PASS from the Judge and no FAIL from Brian, and Brian merges.

## Tracker

The tracker is local markdown, because the notes name league managers and the repo is public (ADR 0021).

- The tracker is `.scratch/<feature>/` at the root, for both apps. See `docs/agents/issue-tracker.md`.
- A feature that both old trackers held keeps a `site/` and a `pipeline/` subfolder, each with its own PRD and `issues/`.
- A new feature has an optional `MAP.md`, `decisions/`, `PRD.md`, `ACCEPTANCE.md`, and `issues/`. Old features keep their shape.

## Where the work sits

`docs/agents/state.md` lists each open feature, its next ticket, and its blocker. An agent new to the repo reads it
after this file, then reads one ticket in the tracker.

## Commits

The prek hook runs `pnpm check:fast` of the site, then `make check-fast` of the pipeline and of the API, before each commit.
Never commit with `--no-verify`.
# Cornerstone API

The FastAPI app serves each client through domain packages and deploys to Fly.
Its product code imports no pipeline code.
API tests reuse pipeline fixtures and README-rule helpers; these test dependencies do not define product ownership.

## Module map

- HTTP composition: the [API owner](src/cornerstone_api/README.md) creates the app and mounts client routes in [app.py](src/cornerstone_api/app.py).
- App state and limits: the [API owner](src/cornerstone_api/README.md) owns client state, access checks, and daily answer allowances.
- Analyzer routes: the [analyzer owner](../../packages/analyzer/README.md) owns trade grades, caches, and persistent grade limits. The API mounts those routes.

## Commands

Run `make help` in `apps/api/` for the app commands.
Run `make check-fast` for lint, types, and rules.
Run `make check` for lint, types, and all tests.

# Simplified Technical English

This is our house style, adapted from ASD-STE100 for software work. It is an adaptation, not
the specification. ASD-STE100 comes from the AeroSpace and Defence Industries Association of
Europe, or ASD. The ASD specification is copyrighted, so this file contains no text from it
and no part of its approved-word dictionary. Download the real specification from
asd-ste100.org if you need the source.

CLAUDE.md carries the short version, and the short version is what runs by default. Read this
file when you rewrite a document. Read it also when you need the complete word list, or when
a rule in CLAUDE.md is unclear.

## Why we do this

Short, plain, consistent sentences are faster to read and harder to misread. Every reader
gets the same meaning from the same words. This matters most for people who read under load:
on call, mid-incident, or three weeks after they last saw the code.

## Scope

The rules apply to:

1. Chat responses.
2. Markdown documents, architecture decision records, plans, and READMEs.
3. Code comments and docstrings.
4. Commit messages, merge request descriptions, and tickets.

## Exemptions

These are outside the rules. Do not rewrite them.

1. **Technical Names.** Nouns that name a real thing: `useEffect`, `Temporal`, `FHIR`,
   `DynamoDB`, `pnpm`, a file path, a branch name, an error code.
2. **Technical Verbs.** Verbs that name a real operation: `commit`, `rebase`, `merge`,
   `deploy`, `mock`, `lint`, `serialize`.
3. **Code.** Identifiers, snippets, and command lines.
4. **Quoted output.** Tool output, logs, and error text stay verbatim.
5. **Jokes and asides.** Banter is exempt. The rules govern technical explanation,
   instructions, and written artifacts. See the humor rule in CLAUDE.md.

An exempt word does not make the sentence around it exempt. Write a plain sentence with the
technical name inside it.

## Rules

### Words

1. Use the plainest word that carries the meaning. See the word list below.
2. Give one word one meaning. Pick a word for a concept and use only that word for it.
3. Give one meaning one word. Do not switch between synonyms for variety.
4. Do not use a noun as a verb, or a verb as a noun. Write "we changed the config", not
   "we actioned the change". Write "the build failed", not "there was a build failure".
5. Spell out an abbreviation the first time you use it, unless it is a Technical Name.
6. Do not use idiom, slang, or metaphor in technical text. "The test is flaky" is fine
   because it is our standard term. "The test is a house of cards" is not.

### Verbs

7. Use the active voice. Write "the migration dropped the column", not "the column was
   dropped by the migration".
8. Use the present tense for how things are. Use the past tense only for what happened.
9. Do not use an `-ing` form as a verb or as a noun. Write "this breaks the build", not
   "this is breaking the build". Write "to parse the file", not "parsing the file".
10. Use an `-ing` or `-ed` form as a plain adjective: "the running process", "the failed
    job".
11. Use the imperative for instructions. Write "run the tests", not "you should run the
    tests" and not "the tests should be run".

### Sentences

12. Keep an instruction to 20 words or fewer.
13. Keep a statement to 25 words or fewer.
14. Write one instruction per sentence. Split "open the file and change line 40" into two
    sentences, or into two numbered steps.
15. Write one topic per sentence.
16. Keep articles. Write "run the script", not "run script".
17. Do not stack more than three nouns. Rewrite "user auth token refresh failure" as "the
    refresh of the user auth token failed".

### Paragraphs

18. Keep a paragraph to six sentences or fewer.
19. Write one topic per paragraph. Start with the topic.
20. Use a numbered list for a sequence. Use a bulleted list for a set.
21. Keep list items parallel. If item 1 starts with a verb, every item starts with a verb.

### Warnings

22. Put the warning before the step it applies to, never after.
23. Write a warning as a plain command: "Stop the server before you run this."
24. Say what happens if the reader ignores it.

### Punctuation

25. Use a hyphen only to join a compound adjective before a noun: "read-only file".
26. Do not use a slash for "or". Write "the branch or the tag", not "the branch/tag".
27. Do not use parentheses for a second thought. Write a second sentence.

## Message structure

These are ours, not ASD's. They govern the shape of a message, not the language in it.

28. Make the first line the next action, not context and not a plan.
29. Number multi-step work. One bounded action per step.
30. Restate where we are every turn: which step, how many remain.
31. Give time estimates in concrete units. "About 15 minutes", not "some work".
32. Say what now works, in concrete terms.
33. Keep a list to five items. Past the fifth item, split the list into "now" and "later".
34. Cut the preamble, the recap, and the closing pleasantries. Start with the answer. Stop
    when the answer is done.
35. State an error as cause and fix. No "uh oh" and no "there seems to be a problem".

## When to relax the rules

1. The reader asks you to explain a topic step by step. Run as long as the topic needs. The
   language rules still hold.
2. A destructive action is next. Confirm first. Safety is more important than brevity.
3. Three turns of "still broken". Stop the edits to the code. Name the assumption that may be
   wrong. Ask one diagnostic question.
4. The request is truly ambiguous. Ask one short question.

## Word list

Use the word on the right.

### Verbs

| Do not use | Use |
| --- | --- |
| accomplish | do |
| ascertain | find out |
| assist | help |
| attempt | try |
| commence | start |
| comprise | have, contain |

| encounter | hit, find |

`execute` and `implement` are Technical Verbs when they name a real operation. In prose, use
`run` and `build`.

### Phrases

| a number of | some, many |

## Examples

Before: "In order to ensure the migration completes successfully, it is necessary to
initially verify that a sufficient number of connections are currently available, and
subsequently the script should be executed by the operator."

After: "First, check that enough connections are free. Then run the script."

Before: "We're currently leveraging the existing user auth token refresh failure handler to
facilitate retries."

After: "The handler for a failed refresh of the user auth token now retries."

Before: "Parsing the response is breaking because the schema was modified by the last
deploy."

After: "The last deploy changed the schema. The parse of the response now fails."
# cornerstone_api

## Knows

- The FastAPI app that serves the trade analyzer to the site of each client.
- At start it reads each folder under `clients/`. A bad `client.toml` stops the start with the file and the key.
- It mounts the analyzer routes of the `analyzer` package at `/clients/<slug>/`. The old paths with no client answer as `cpc`.
- It mounts the eggs routes of the `eggs` package at `/clients/<slug>/eggs/` for each client of the package, with one SQLite file per client in `CORNERSTONE_EGGS_DIR`.
- The ask route of the front door at `/clients/<slug>/ask`, behind the passphrase. One Jev request routes each typed question, and the route table in `ask.py` reads the answers. `ask_wording.py` holds every word sent to Jev. An honest miss writes one entry in the miss log, one SQLite file per client in `CORNERSTONE_ASK_DIR`, kept 90 days (ADR 0031).
- The trade Topics of the front door at `/clients/<slug>/trade-check` and `/clients/<slug>/trade-ideas`, behind the passphrase, in `trade_topics.py`. A typed trade check has one Jev request that picks the player of each side from the real rosters, with its words in `trade_wording.py`. An unsure pick gives the form of the Trade page. Each route streams a plain step for each stage of the Advisor, then the whole Answer, in the event stream of the AI SDK. Trade ideas runs whatever the `finder` flag says. Sell high at `/clients/<slug>/sell-high` streams the same way, with the sell high press of the `analyzer` package.
- The free answer of the ask box at `/clients/<slug>/ask/free`, behind the passphrase. The route runs again first, so only a question that Jev routes to a free answer reaches Claude. Claude Sonnet 5.5 runs at `low` effort through Pydantic AI, with the tools of `free_tools.py` over the saved weeks of this season and at most 4 tool calls. The text streams through `VercelAIAdapter` to `useChat` of the site. After the last word, one Jev request checks each sentence against the tool results, with one rewrite and then the honest miss. `free_wording.py` holds every word sent to Claude and to Jev for it. Each typed question carries the earlier turns of its Thread, cut to about 8,000 tokens, as Jev state for the route and as earlier messages for Claude, with a cache mark. The check never reads them. `chat_turns.py` holds them and their words.
- The refresh route that a daily cron pings.
- The passphrase check of each client, from `CORNERSTONE_PASSPHRASE_<SLUG>`, the commissioner key check of each client of the eggs package, from `CORNERSTONE_COMMISSIONER_KEY_<SLUG>`, the rate limit of each address, the limit of the egg check of each address, the state of each client, and the settings from the environment. [caps.py](caps.py) owns daily answer allowances per team and local calendar day. [test_caps.py](../../tests/test_caps.py) checks team isolation and the next-day reset.
- The terms are in `GLOSSARY.md`.

## Ports

- It takes the `Jev` port of the `league` package for the ask route, the trade picks, and the check of the free answer. `create_app` takes a `jev`, so a test gives `FakeJev`. The free answer runs the model of its Pydantic AI agent, and a test sets `app.state.free_model` to a function model of Pydantic AI.

## Does not do

- It holds no grade rule and no prompt of the trade analyzer. The [analyzer owner](../../../../packages/analyzer/README.md) holds them, with the grade limit and the caches. The only prompt here is the free answer of `free_wording.py`.
- It imports no pipeline code. Only its tests read the fixtures of the pipeline tests.
- It imports nothing from the output layer of ADR 0010, so it writes no page.
